title: The Lighthouse · 8
paragraphs: They feel nothing over there, Cam thought, watching the shore, which rose and fell and grew steadily further off and more peaceful. Her hand drew a furrow through the sea, while her mind turned the green swirls and streaks into patterns. Numb and muffled, she wandered in her imagination through that underwater world where pearls clung in clusters to white branches of spray, where, in the green light, your whole mind was changed, and your body glowed half transparent inside a green cloak.

Then the swirl around her hand died away. The water stopped rushing past; the world was full of small creaks and squeaks. You could hear the waves breaking and lapping at the side of the boat as if they lay at anchor in a harbor. Everything drew very near. James had kept his eyes on the sail until it had become like a person he knew, and now it sagged completely, so they came to a halt, flapping about and waiting for a breeze in the hot sun, miles from land, miles from the Lighthouse. The whole world seemed to stand still. The Lighthouse stopped moving, and the line of the far shore stayed fixed. As the sun grew hotter, they all seemed to draw very close together and to sense one another’s presence, which they had nearly forgotten. Macalister’s fishing line dropped straight down into the water. But Mr. Ramsay kept reading, his legs tucked up under him.

The book he was reading was a small, glossy one, its covers speckled like a plover’s egg. Every now and then, as they drifted in that dreadful calm, he turned a page. To James it seemed that every page was turned with a particular gesture meant for him—sometimes assertive, sometimes commanding, sometimes designed to make people feel sorry for him. And the whole time his father was reading and turning those little pages one after another, James was dreading the moment he would look up and say something sharp to him about one thing or another. Why were they hanging about here? he would ask, or something just as unreasonable. And if he does, James thought, I’ll take a knife and strike him to the heart.

This old symbol—taking a knife and striking his father to the heart—he had always kept. Only now that he was older, as he sat glaring at his father in helpless fury, it was not the man himself he wanted to kill, not that old man reading. It was the thing that came down on him—perhaps without his knowing: that fierce, sudden harpy with black wings, its claws and beak all hard and cold, which struck and struck at you (he could feel that beak on his bare legs, where it had struck him as a child) and then flew off; and there he was again, an old man, very sad, reading his book. That was what he would kill; that was what he would strike to the heart. Whatever he did with his life—(and he felt he might do anything, as he looked at the Lighthouse and the distant shore)—whether he went into business or a bank, or became a lawyer, or ran some enterprise, that was what he would fight, what he would hunt down and stamp out: tyranny, despotism, as he called it—forcing people to do what they didn’t want to do, taking away their right to speak. How could any of them say, But I won’t, when he said, Come to the Lighthouse. Do this. Fetch me that. The black wings spread; the hard beak tore. And then, a moment later, there he was, sitting reading; and he might look up—you never could tell—perfectly reasonably. He might chat with the Macalisters. He might be pressing a gold coin into the hand of some freezing old woman in the street, James thought; he might be cheering at some fishermen’s sports day; he might be flinging his arms about in excitement. Or he might sit at the head of the table without a word from one end of dinner to the other. Yes, James thought, while the boat slapped and lazed about in the hot sun: there was a wasteland of snow and rock, very lonely and stern; and there, he had begun to feel quite often lately, whenever his father said something that took the others by surprise, were only two sets of footprints—his and his father’s. Only they knew each other. Then what was this terror, this hatred? He turned back among the many leaves the past had folded inside him, peering into the heart of that forest where light and shadow so dapple each other that every shape is warped, and you stumble along, now with the sun in your eyes, now in dark shade. He was searching for an image that would cool his feeling, set it apart, and round it off into something solid. Suppose, then, that when he was a child sitting helpless in his baby carriage, or on somebody’s lap, he had seen a cart crush someone’s foot, without meaning to, innocently? Suppose he had seen the foot first, smooth and whole in the grass; then the wheel; then that same foot, purple and crushed. But the wheel was innocent. And so now, when his father came striding down the hall early in the morning, banging on their doors to get them up to go to the Lighthouse, it came down over his foot, over Cam’s foot, over anyone’s foot. You just sat and watched.

But whose foot did he mean, and in what garden had it all happened? Because these scenes had their settings: trees growing there; flowers; a particular light; a few figures. Everything tended to arrange itself in a garden free of all this gloom and all this flinging about of hands, where people talked in ordinary voices. All day long they went in and out. An old woman was gossiping in the kitchen; the breeze sucked the blinds in and out; everything was blowing and growing. And at night a very thin yellow veil, like a vine leaf, would be drawn over all those plates and bowls and the tall, waving red and yellow flowers. At night things grew quieter and darker. But the leaf-like veil was so delicate that lamps lifted it and voices wrinkled it; through it he could make out a figure bending down, and hear some dress rustling, some chain jingling, as it came near and went away.

It was in this world that the wheel had passed over the person’s foot. Something, he remembered, hung over him and darkened; it wouldn’t move. Something was brandished in the air; something dry and sharp came down, even there, like a blade, like a curved sword, cutting through the leaves and flowers of even that happy world and making them wither and drop.
“It’s going to rain,” he remembered his father saying. “You won’t be able to go to the Lighthouse.”
In those days the Lighthouse had been a silvery, misty tower with a yellow eye that opened, suddenly and gently, in the evening. Now—

James looked at the Lighthouse. He could make out the whitewashed rocks and the tower, bare and upright. He could see it was banded in black and white; he could see its windows; he could even see laundry laid out to dry on the rocks. So that was the Lighthouse, was it?

No—the other one was the Lighthouse as well. Nothing was ever just one thing. The other one was the Lighthouse too. At times you could barely make it out across the bay. In the evenings you would look up and see the eye open and close, and the light seemed to reach all the way to them in that airy, sunlit garden where they were sitting.

But he caught himself. Whenever he said “they” or “a person” and began to hear someone rustling in or tinkling out, he grew intensely aware of whoever might be in the room. Now it was his father. The tension became unbearable. Any moment now, if no breeze came, his father would clap his book shut and say, “What’s the matter now? Why are we dawdling about here, eh?”—just as once before he had brought his blade down among them on the terrace, and she had gone rigid, and if an axe had been within reach, or a knife, or anything sharp, James would have grabbed it and stabbed his father through the heart. His mother had gone rigid all over; then her arm had loosened, so that he felt she was no longer listening to him, and somehow she had got up and gone off and left him there—helpless, absurd, sitting on the floor gripping a pair of scissors.

There wasn’t a breath of wind. Water chuckled and gurgled in the bottom of the boat, where three or four mackerel flapped their tails up and down in a puddle too shallow to cover them. Mr. Ramsay (James hardly dared glance at him) might wake up at any moment, close his book, and say something sharp. But for now he was reading, and so James went on thinking, stealthily, as if he were tiptoeing barefoot down the stairs, afraid a creaking board would wake a watchdog: what was she like, and where had she gone that day? He started following her from one room to the next, until at last they reached a room where, in a bluish light, as though reflected off a great many china dishes, she was talking to someone, and he listened. She was speaking to a servant, just saying whatever came into her mind. “We shall need a big dish tonight. Where is it—the blue dish?” Only she told the truth; only to her could he tell it. Perhaps that was the source of her endless attraction for him: she was someone you could say anything to, whatever came into your head. But the whole time he was thinking of her, he could feel his father following his thought, shadowing it, making it tremble and stumble.

In the end he stopped thinking. He just sat there in the sun, his hand on the tiller, staring at the Lighthouse, unable to move, unable to brush off these grains of misery that kept settling on his mind one by one. It was as if a rope held him there, a rope his father had knotted, and the only way to escape was to take a knife and plunge it in. … But just then the sail swung slowly round and slowly filled; the boat seemed to shake herself, then to move off, half conscious, still in her sleep; and then she woke up and shot through the waves. The relief was enormous. They all seemed to move apart again and relax, and the fishing lines stretched tight at a slant over the side. But his father did not stir. He simply lifted his right hand high in the air, mysteriously, and let it drop back onto his knee, as if he were conducting some secret symphony.
